stories.headline: Update: Taiwan President Vows No Provocation, No Surrender of Sovereignty After Trump-Xi Summit
stories.summary:
Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te issued his first public response to the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, declaring that Taiwan "will not provoke, will not escalate conflict, but will not under pressure give up national sovereignty and dignity." Writing on Facebook, Lai reiterated that Taiwan — officially the Republic of China — is already a sovereign, independent democratic country and that there is therefore no "Taiwan independence issue" requiring formal declaration.

The statement came after Chinese President Xi Jinping told Trump that Taiwan was "the most important issue" in U.S.-China relations and that mishandling it could lead to conflict. Trump, speaking to Fox News after leaving Beijing, warned Taiwan against seeking independence, saying "I'm not looking to have somebody go independent," while also telling reporters he made "no commitment either way" to Beijing.

Lai said Taiwan is willing to pursue "healthy and orderly exchanges and dialogue with China on the premise of equality and dignity" but rejected Beijing's use of "unification" framing as a vehicle for coercion. Beijing, which considers Taiwan a breakaway province, has labeled Lai a "troublemaker" and has not ruled out the use of force to take the island.

The exchange highlights the renewed fragility of cross-strait relations following the summit. The U.S. remains Taiwan's largest arms supplier under the Taiwan Relations Act; the Trump administration approved $11 billion in arms sales to Taipei in December. Some Trump advisers have privately warned that Xi may view the summit's outcome as an opening to more aggressive moves toward Taiwan within the next five years.

stories.headline: Trump Drops $10 Billion Lawsuit Against IRS Over Tax Return Leak
stories.summary:
President Trump, his two eldest sons, and the Trump Organization voluntarily dismissed their $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS and Treasury Department on Monday, according to a filing in a Miami federal court. The suit had alleged that the IRS improperly leaked Trump's tax returns in 2019.

The dismissal is notable for its timing: Trump has been publicly weighing the creation of a $1.776 billion taxpayer-funded compensation fund for individuals who claim they were wrongfully targeted by the Biden administration, including January 6 defendants. The proposed fund reflects Trump's longstanding assertion that the Biden-era Justice Department was weaponized against his allies.

Supporters of the dismissal argue it clears the decks for a broader political remedy — the compensation fund — rather than a narrow legal one. Critics contend that a presidential administration dropping a personal lawsuit while simultaneously considering a taxpayer-funded fund for political allies raises serious conflict-of-interest concerns.

The voluntary dismissal means no court ruling on the merits of the IRS leak claim will be issued. The move was reported by five outlets including ABC News, Axios, Bloomberg, and NBC News.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Joins 'Rededicate 250' Faith Rally on National Mall, Recites Scripture
stories.summary:
President Trump appeared at the "Rededicate 250" Christian prayer rally on the National Mall Sunday alongside Cabinet members, reciting a passage from 2 Chronicles 7 in a video address aired to the crowd. The verse — "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then will I hear from heaven" — is frequently cited by evangelical Christians as a call for national spiritual renewal.

The event was organized as part of celebrations leading up to the 250th anniversary of American independence and drew thousands of attendees to the Mall. It is among the largest faith-oriented political gatherings in Washington in recent years, with the president's participation lending it significant official visibility.

Supporters framed Trump's involvement as an affirmation of the administration's alignment with Christian conservative values and the broader religious freedom agenda that has animated much of his political base. Critics and civil liberties advocates raised concerns about the blurring of lines between official governmental participation and a sectarian religious event.

The rally was covered by 19 outlets across the political spectrum, making it one of the most widely reported domestic stories of the day.

stories.headline: Pentagon Signs AI Contracts With Google, OpenAI, Amazon and Others to Build 'AI-First' Military
stories.summary:
The Pentagon announced Friday it has signed expanded contracts with eight major technology companies — Google, OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and startup Reflection — authorizing AI tools for any "lawful operational use" across the U.S. military. Defense officials said the agreements are designed to accelerate the transformation of the armed forces into an "AI-first fighting force" and to avoid over-reliance on any single vendor.

The announcement formalizes several arrangements already in use; more than one million Defense Department personnel have accessed the military's AI platform since its launch last year, with officials saying it has cut many tasks "from months to days." The deals represent the most sweeping institutionalization of commercial AI in U.S. military history.

Notably absent from the agreements is Anthropic, whose CEO Dario Amodei had publicly warned that powerful AI could be used for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," and the company is now suing the government over what it describes as retaliation. That legal challenge is expected to reach court in September.

The move comes amid growing debate — including from over 60 Trump allies who sent a letter Monday urging mandatory White House review of powerful AI models before release — about how rapidly the U.S. government should deploy artificial intelligence without formal safety vetting.

stories.headline: Israeli Forces Board Gaza-Bound Flotilla in International Waters Near Cyprus
stories.summary:
Israeli military commandos boarded multiple vessels from the Global Sumud Flotilla on Monday as the convoy of more than 50 boats attempted to break Israel's maritime blockade of Gaza, according to activists who streamed the operation live. The interception occurred roughly 250 nautical miles west of Cyprus, in international waters. Israel's foreign ministry had no immediate comment but previously described the flotilla as "a provocation" involving "two violent Turkish groups."

This is the second interception of the same flotilla. In April, Israeli forces stopped 22 boats near Crete, detaining about 175 activists, nearly all of whom were released on a Greek island the following day amid international condemnation. The remaining boats regrouped in Turkey before departing again last week.

Activists say they are attempting to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza's 2.1 million residents, most of whom are displaced despite a ceasefire agreed seven months ago. Israel maintains the maritime blockade is lawful and that Gaza is "flooded with aid." The UN disputes that characterization, noting that restrictions on spare parts, fuel, and equipment continue to undermine humanitarian operations, and that 14 percent of approved supplies were turned back at border crossings.

The interception is likely to intensify international scrutiny of Israel's blockade policy at a moment when the Gaza war, now in its twentieth month, has killed more than 72,760 people according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Diplomatic fallout from the April incident — which drew widespread condemnation — suggests the boarding of a larger convoy will generate significant international reaction.

stories.headline: Kenya Paralyzed by Nationwide Transport Strike Over Record Fuel Prices
stories.summary:
Thousands of Kenyan commuters were stranded Monday as public transport operators launched a nationwide strike to protest fuel prices that hit record highs after the government raised petroleum costs by more than 20 percent last week. Key roads in the capital Nairobi were largely empty, schools sent students home, and businesses in parts of the city remained shut. Police used tear gas against demonstrators who barricaded roads and lit fires.

The price surge is directly linked to the disruption of Gulf oil supply routes following the U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran that began February 28. Although a ceasefire was declared, the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passes — remains blocked, keeping global fuel prices elevated. Kenya, like many African nations, depends heavily on fuel imports from the Gulf.

The Transport Sector Alliance, which organized the shutdown, called on all vehicle users — including private motorists, matatus, and truckers — to stay off the roads, framing the action as a national crisis rather than a labor dispute alone. The alliance is demanding a 35 percent reduction in fuel prices and accuses the government of failing to shield citizens from a broader cost-of-living crisis.

Treasury Minister John Mbadi called the price increase "unfortunate" but said the strike was "completely uncalled for," arguing that Kenya cannot solve a global problem through domestic measures. The government had already cut VAT on fuel from 16 to 8 percent through July, but activists say the relief is insufficient. The crisis illustrates the cascading economic consequences of the Iran conflict for developing nations far from the Middle East.

stories.headline: Update: Bangkok Train Crash Driver Tested Positive for Drugs, Charged With Reckless Driving
stories.summary:
Thai police announced Monday that the freight train driver whose locomotive struck a public bus in Bangkok on Saturday, killing eight people, has tested positive for drugs and been formally charged with reckless driving. The bus had stalled on the Asoke-Din Daeng railway crossing due to heavy traffic that prevented the safety barriers from lowering in time. The bus burst into flames on impact; dozens more were injured.

Both the bus driver and the crossing guard responsible for manually lowering the barrier have also been charged, authorities said. Preliminary data from the train's black box showed the emergency braking system was activated only about 100 meters from the bus — too short a distance to prevent the collision. Thai rail authorities have ordered mandatory drug and alcohol tests for all train drivers and railway staff before their shifts.

Experts say the crash reflects deep structural risks at the crossing, which sees an estimated 100,000 road vehicles per day — well above the safety threshold for such junctions. The tracks predate the surrounding road network, and urban growth has created what one structural engineer called "risk normalisation" — a cultural acceptance of hazardous conditions that persists until a catastrophe occurs.

The disaster has intensified public pressure on Thai authorities to modernize railway infrastructure and enforce safety standards more rigorously. District officials and transport regulators are reviewing crossing safety across Bangkok.

stories.headline: Senate Unanimously Votes to Withhold Members' Pay During Government Shutdowns
stories.summary:
The U.S. Senate unanimously approved a bipartisan resolution Thursday that would withhold senators' salaries during government shutdowns, directing the secretary of the Senate to hold lawmakers' pay until funding is restored. The measure, sponsored by Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), is intended to create a financial incentive for Congress to avoid shutdowns after a string of record-breaking funding lapses over the past year.

The resolution comes in the wake of two shutdowns that caused severe hardship for tens of thousands of federal workers. A 76-day partial shutdown at the Department of Homeland Security — the longest agency funding lapse in U.S. history — ended only last month, following a 43-day full government shutdown that also set a record. The Constitution requires lawmakers to be paid regardless of government operations, meaning senators continued to receive their $174,000 annual salaries while federal employees went without paychecks.

The resolution does not apply to the House of Representatives. Kennedy said the House's "business is the House's business" while acknowledging significant tensions between the chambers. Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) had previously proposed a constitutional amendment to permanently require lawmakers to forfeit pay during shutdowns, but acknowledged that path would take far longer given the requirement that three-fourths of states ratify any amendment.

The measure takes effect the day after the November 3 general election. Critics note that many senators are independently wealthy, limiting the practical deterrent effect, but supporters argue it establishes an important principle of shared sacrifice between lawmakers and the federal workforce they oversee.
